reason: Giving the wandering stones fire seems like a direct way to work toward gathering a sun.
expectation: I expect the stones to become fiery, perhaps contributing to a sun; the exact result is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: The storm might gather the stones, but the chapter specifically suggests giving some pieces fire.

effect: The stones now carry fire, so gathering them seems like a plausible next step toward a sun.
reaction: The image of flying fragments carrying little lights is satisfying.
reason: The first storm gathers things in its reach, so it may bring the burning stones together.
expectation: I expect the storm to gather the burning stones, perhaps forming a sun or an intermediate object.

alternatives.reason: The storm could also gather unlit stones, but the burning stones seem more relevant to making a sun.

effect: The storm gathered the burning stones into a sun, revealing a new goal to gather a galaxy.
reaction: The fires crowding into one light made the result feel satisfying.
reason: The storm has already gathered burning stones, so gathering the remaining sky stones seems worth trying for the galaxy.
expectation: I expect the storm to gather the sky stones into some larger formation, though I don't know whether it will be a galaxy.

alternatives.reason: Water might cool the burning stones toward a gentler light, but I want to pursue the new gathering goal first.

effect: The storm gathered unlit stones into a rocky world rather than a galaxy, opening several new combinations.
reaction: The stones pressing together into a hot world was an interesting surprise.
reason: A rocky world paired with the sun may produce the gentler light the goal asks for.
expectation: I expect the sun to illuminate the rocky world, perhaps making a moon-like light, though the result is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Water might cool the burning stones, but the world and sun seem a more direct route to reflected light.

effect: The sun and rocky world produced day and night, not a gentler light, so I will try cooling the burning stones instead.
reaction: The turning world was a clear, satisfying explanation of day and night.
reason: Water may cool the burning stones into something less bright.
expectation: I expect the water to cool or dim the stones, perhaps producing a gentler light, though I am unsure.

alternatives.reason: Water on the rocky world could also make progress, but seems less directly related to light.

effect: Water quenched a burning stone, leaving a pale fragment that might reflect sunlight.
reaction: The distinction between its own light and reflected light is a useful clue.
reason: Pairing the pale stone with the sun may give the darkness its gentler light.
expectation: I expect the stone to reflect sunlight, perhaps becoming a moon-like light.

effect: The pale stone reflected sunlight to become the Moon, completing the gentler-light goal; gathering a galaxy remains.
reaction: The explanation that the Moon gives back sunlight is clear and satisfying.
reason: Burning stones already carry individual lights, so combining them with air might help scatter or gather lights toward a galaxy.
expectation: I expect the air to spread or change the burning stones, perhaps creating a group of lights; I'm unsure how this leads to a galaxy.

alternatives.reason: Water on the rocky world could develop the world, but seems less directly related to the galaxy goal.

effect: The burning stones became a starfield, suggesting the storm could gather its scattered lights into a galaxy.
reaction: The scattered fragments becoming stars is an evocative continuation of the myth.
reason: The first storm has gathered stones before, so it seems useful for gathering the starfield.
expectation: I expect the storm to gather the stars into a galaxy, though the result could be an intermediate formation.

effect: The storm gathered the starfield into a galaxy, completing the final goal.
reaction: The image of a spiral resolving into individual suns was satisfying.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making day and night was most worthwhile: the turning world gave a clear explanation of why places alternate between light and shadow.

leastWorthwhile.text: Cooling the burning stones felt somewhat like a guess after the sun-and-world combination did not produce the gentler light.

surprise.text: Gathering unlit stones made a hot rocky world rather than the galaxy I had expected.

arbitrary.text: Using air to scatter burning stones into stars felt more like a mythic recipe than a clear physical inference, though the result explicitly framed it as myth.

continue.text: Yes. The concise combinations and the clear explanation of reflected moonlight made me curious to see how the world develops.
